title: Unusual mediastinal dumbbell tumor mimicking an aggressive malignancy
case_text:
A 22-year-old female, farmer by occupation, presented with complaints of chest pain and progressive weakness of left lower limb that had persisted for 3 months. There was no history of fever, weight loss, or trauma. The general physical examination was unremarkable. Respiratory system examination revealed dullness on percussion and tenderness in left infraclavicular, suprascapular, and interscapular regions. The routine laboratory investigations were normal.
Radiographs of chest, performed in posterior-anterior (PA) and lateral projections, demonstrated well-defined homogenous soft tissue opacity in the posterior mediastinum. There was erosion of the 4th rib posteriorly, scalloping of superior margin of 5th rib, and widened fourth intercostal space [Figure 1a and b]. Contrast enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the thorax revealed a well-defined, multiloculated cystic mass in the left paravertebral space, extending into the spinal canal by causing erosion of the adjoining pedicle and lamina of fourth thoracic vertebra. There was erosion of the overlying 4th rib with scalloping of the 5th rib and widened intervening intercostal space [Figures 2 and 3].
Based on the imaging findings, the possible differential diagnosis included neurogenic tumors, aggressive malignant masses like round cell tumors (Ewing's sarcoma, primitive neuroectodermal tumors, and others), lymphoma, or metastasis. Since the mass was predominantly cystic with multiloculated appearance and considering the occupation of the patient, hydatid cyst was also considered a possible differential diagnosis.
The serological test with enzyme linked immunosorbant assay (ELISA) was positive for echinococcosis, thus suggesting hydatid cyst as a possible etiology. The patient was operated and the cystic mass along with the involved 4th rib were completely excised. The diagnosis was confirmed macroscopically preoperatively and by histopathological studies postoperatively. Postoperative recovery was uneventful and the patient was discharged and put on adjuvant chemotherapy with mebendazole for 2 years. The patient was monitored with routine follow-ups for 5 years with no evidence of recurrence.

1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Echinococcosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: mediastinal dumbbell hydatid cyst with intraspinal extension
